title: Veteran Benefits
subtitle: You can serve twenty-three years and still not know the form number

blocks.text: Somewhere in Canada tonight, a former combat engineer has two bad knees, hearing loss from the ranges, and a firm belief that none of it counts because he never deployed anywhere more exciting than Meaford in March.
He is wrong, and it is costing him money.

VAC publishes every program and every rule. The hard part is finding the right door after a long week. This module gives you the map: who counts, what may fit, which program unlocks the others, what to do with a lump sum, and what to do when the decision letter says no.
Knowing that your service counts can turn years of quiet pain into treatment and support you have earned.
blocks.detail: Most Veterans who screen themselves out never deployed and assume that settles it. It does not.
blocks.extra: Section 02 shows who VAC counts as a Veteran.

sections.title: Who VAC Counts as a Veteran

blocks.text: For most VAC programs, a Veteran is someone who completed basic training and was honourably released. That is the whole test.

items.title: No deployment required
items.text: You do not have to have served overseas.

items.title: No combat required
items.text: A training injury in Wainwright can be service-related.

items.title: Reserve service counts
items.text: Class A, B and C, Primary Reserve, Rangers and COATS all matter.

items.title: Families have rights too
items.text: Partners, survivors, orphans and caregivers may qualify in their own right.

blocks.text: There is no minimum-drama threshold. VAC is not grading how impressive the story sounds. The useful question is simpler: is the condition connected to service?

items.title: “I never deployed, so I do not qualify.”
items.text: Service-related does not mean combat-related. Hearing loss from the ranges, a back injury from a load or a knee that went during PT may count. Reserve service counts too.

blocks.text: An approved disability benefit, Pain and Suffering Compensation or a Disability Pension, is more than a payment. It can unlock the Treatment Benefits Program and the health care card for that condition: hearing aids, physiotherapy and prescriptions.
Plain English: sequence beats speed. Apply for the key first, or alongside the programs it may unlock.
VAC: Disability benefits
Most VAC support fits into one of these six rooms. Start with the need, then learn the program name.

items.title: Recognition
list: PSC: today’s main tax-free disability benefit
Disability Pension: generally the older system
APSC: for a permanent barrier to rebuilding civilian life
Critical Injury Benefit: for a sudden, severe service injury
items.detail: For an illness or injury connected to service.

items.title: Income
list: Rehabilitation: medical, emotional and job support
IRB: taxable monthly income while taking part in rehab
CF Income Support: a low-income floor while job-searching
War Veterans Allowance: income support that also carries treatment benefits
items.detail: For money coming in while you rebuild.

items.title: Health
list: Prescriptions, dental, vision and daily-living aids
A VAC health care card after qualifying
Many providers bill Medavie Blue Cross directly
Some mental-health treatment starts as soon as you apply

items.title: Home
list: VIP may fund snow removal and yard work
It may also fund housekeeping, meals and personal care
Apply for VIP with the disability application when needed
The Caregiver Recognition Benefit is paid to the caregiver

list: Food, shelter and clothing
Urgent uninsured medical or dental needs
No other VAC benefit is required
Veterans, spouses, survivors and orphans may qualify
items.detail: For an urgent problem affecting health or safety.

blocks.text: For certain mental-health conditions, treatment coverage can begin as soon as you apply for a disability benefit. You do not have to wait for the decision. VAC Assistance Service: 1‑800‑268‑7708, 24/7.

items.title: “It has been twenty years. That ship has sailed.”
items.text: Disability benefits have no general application deadline. Other programs do. ETB has a hard deadline, and funeral and burial assistance closes one year after death. Check each program.

blocks.text: Income from the Rehabilitation Program works differently from a disability award. The Income Replacement Benefit is taxable and is meant to bring your total income to at least 90% of your gross pre-release military salary while you take part in rehabilitation. Other income, like a pension or CPP, is counted against it.
My VAC Account

sections.title: Two Systems, and What a Lump Sum Does to Your Money

blocks.text: Your neighbour may receive a monthly cheque while you were offered a lump sum. That does not mean one file is wrong. You may be under different programs.

items.title: Disability Pension
list: Usually wartime service and applications before April 1, 2006
Paid monthly for life
Not taxable
May unlock treatment benefits for the approved condition

items.title: Pain and Suffering Compensation
list: Applications from April 1, 2019 onward
Monthly for life, or a lump sum
Not taxable
May unlock treatment benefits for the approved condition

blocks.text: VAC decides whether you qualify. It does not choose what works best with your debts, taxes or income-tested benefits. That is your second calculation.

A lump sum can clear expensive debt in one move, but the money can also be spent early. Monthly payments create income you cannot spend in advance, but offer less money upfront. Neither choice is automatically “responsible.” They solve different problems.
If you choose the lump sum, give every dollar a job before it lands. Try it with an example amount, then your own.
Give a lump-sum award a job
blocks.extra: Enter the award and leave the baseline at $0. Assign every dollar until nothing is left without a job.

items.title: A $60,000 example
items.text: AWARD RECEIVED|BASELINE (LEAVE AT $0)|This is an example amount, not a VAC rate. Check your own decision letter, and talk to a free financial counsellor before a large lump sum lands.

items.title: “A big tax-free payment means I can stop budgeting.”
items.text: Tax-free is not limitless. Without a plan, a lump sum can disappear into small purchases in a year and leave the original problem standing.

sections.title: Your First Application, Step by Step

blocks.text: Six steps. The order is the point.

items.title: Start online
items.text: Open My VAC Account, then run the ten-minute Benefits Navigator. Collect every result before deciding what fits.

items.title: Document the condition
items.text: See your medical provider before applying. The file needs the condition as it is today. The file is not impressed by what you meant.

items.title: Bring in free help
items.text: Call a Legion or War Amps Service Officer, VAC, a CAF Transition Centre or Service Canada. They know which document tends to wander off.

items.title: Apply side by side
items.text: Where allowed, submit related applications together. If home help is needed, ask about filing VIP with the disability application.

items.title: Check the service record
items.text: VAC normally requests your service health records. You should confirm whether a CF98 or DND 663 incident form exists.

items.title: Use the decision letter
items.text: If approved, check what it unlocks. If denied or deferred, the evidence list shows the gap and becomes your roadmap.

blocks.text: Build your starter file

items.title: Service number
items.text: With your enrolment and release dates. Check old photos, pay stubs and release papers.

items.title: Release documents
items.text: Your release message or certificate shows how and when you left.

items.title: Incident reports
items.text: Any CF98 or DND 663 forms filled out when you were hurt.

items.title: Medical records
items.text: Current civilian records that describe the condition as it is today.

items.title: Statements
items.text: Short written accounts from people who served with you and saw what happened.

items.title: Deposit details
items.text: Banking details and clear scans of every page, ready to upload.

blocks.text: Legion and War Amps Service Officers can build the application with you, even if you are not a member. VAC, CAF Transition Centre and Service Canada staff can also help. None of this costs a dollar.

items.title: The Modest File
items.text: Describing your worst day as “not that bad.” Understatement is a fine personal quality and a terrible filing strategy. Describe the bad days accurately, including what you can no longer do.

items.title: The Shoebox Archive
items.text: Every document exists. None of them are anywhere. This turns a two-hour task into a three-week task and is entirely solved by one afternoon with a scanner.

items.title: The Sequential Applicant
items.text: One form, wait, decision, next form, wait. Where parallel applications are allowed, using them can move your start date months earlier.

blocks.text: VAC: Application help

sections.title: Dennis, the Garage, and Twelve Years He Thought Did Not Count

blocks.text: Meet Dennis
paragraphs: Dennis is sixty-one and lives outside Sudbury. He spent twelve years as a Reserve combat engineer: weekends, summer taskings and two Class B stints he mostly remembers for the food. He has ringing in his ears from demolition training and two bad knees he blames on everything else.

His goal is modest. He wants to keep shovelling his own driveway and hear his grandkids at dinner. A guy at the arena told him the VAC process was a nightmare. The guy at the arena had never applied either.
His daughter sits him down with the Benefits Navigator. In twenty minutes he learns that Reserve service counts, and that he does not need a deployment to have a service injury.

Then the form asks for his service number. Dennis has no idea where it is and is ready to close the laptop. His daughter waits. He decides to look for one more hour. The number turns up on the back of a photo, in a box, in the garage, behind the snowblower.

He does the rest in order: a hearing test and a doctor’s visit, then the Legion Service Officer in town, free of charge. The officer has him send the Veterans Independence Program form at the same time, because of the long driveway and a Sudbury winter arriving on schedule.

The ringing ears are approved. The knees are put on hold until a specialist report arrives, and the letter names the exact report that is missing. The approval brings the health care card and the hearing aids he had put off for three years. At dinner that Sunday, he hears every word his grandkids say.

items.title: NAVIGATOR
items.text: Reserve service counts

items.title: GARAGE
items.text: Service number found

items.title: SAME DAY
items.text: Disability and VIP sent together

blocks.text: Dennis got hearing aids and a clear next step for his knees by applying instead of screening himself out.
blocks.detail: A free Service Officer and the right order of steps can do the same for your own file.
blocks.extra: Section 07 shows what to do when the letter says “not yet.”

sections.title: When the Letter Says No, or Not Yet

blocks.text: Dennis’s knees were not refused. They were put on hold for one missing report. Many decisions work like that. The letter lists the evidence VAC used and what was missing, which makes it the most useful page in your file.

items.title: Read the evidence list
items.text: Find the exact reason and the missing proof. Ask VAC to explain anything unclear before you act.

items.title: Send what is missing
items.text: A specialist report or a witness statement can sometimes settle a deferred claim without a formal review.

items.title: Ask for a departmental review
items.text: If you have new evidence or think VAC made an error, VAC can look at its own decision again.

items.title: Go to the Board
items.text: The Veterans Review and Appeal Board is independent of VAC. Lawyers from the Bureau of Pensions Advocates can represent you there for free.

items.title: Reassess if it worsens
items.text: If an approved condition gets worse, ask for a reassessment. Your award can go up.

blocks.text: If you feel you were treated unfairly by VAC, as opposed to simply disagreeing with a decision, the Veterans Ombud is a separate, free office that looks into complaints.

items.title: “I was denied once, so that is the end of it.”
items.text: The decision letter tells you what evidence VAC used. That can guide a departmental review, VRAB appeal, new application or reassessment if the condition worsens.

blocks.text: VAC: Reviews and appeals

sections.title: Quick Check: Choose the Best Next Move

items.title: What is the basic test VAC uses for who is a Veteran?
items.detail: For most programs, completing basic training and being honourably released. Deployment and combat are not required.

items.title: Why does the first disability approval matter so much?
items.detail: It can unlock the Treatment Benefits Program and the health care card for that condition, such as hearing aids or physiotherapy.

items.title: When can treatment for some mental-health conditions start?
items.detail: As soon as you apply for a disability benefit, without waiting for the decision.

items.title: A $40,000 lump sum arrives. You give $12,000 to debt, $10,000 to an emergency fund and $15,000 to savings. How much has no job yet?
What does the Income Replacement Benefit aim for?
items.detail: A total income of at least 90% of your gross pre-release military salary while you take part in rehabilitation. It is taxable.

items.title: Who can represent you for free at the Veterans Review and Appeal Board?
items.detail: Lawyers from the Bureau of Pensions Advocates.

items.title: An approved condition is getting worse. What can you ask for?
items.detail: A reassessment, which can raise your award.

sections.title: Your Action (Fill Out Form): Your Entitlement Map

blocks.text: This week: set up or log into My VAC Account, run the Benefits Navigator and write down every program it returns. Then book one call with a Legion or War Amps Service Officer, or VAC at 1‑866‑522‑2122, and ask which to apply for first and which can go in at the same time. Keep your service number, health details and banking out of this form.
Do not screen yourself out.
blocks.detail: Completed basic training and released honourably? Find the anchor entitlement, apply side by side where possible, have a free Service Officer check the file and treat a “not yet” letter as a list of what to send next.

items.title: PSC
items.text: Pain and Suffering Compensation. The current tax-free disability benefit, monthly for life or lump sum.

items.title: APSC
items.text: Additional Pain and Suffering Compensation. Monthly payment for a permanent barrier to re-establishment.

items.title: IRB
items.text: Income Replacement Benefit. Taxable monthly support tied to VAC rehabilitation.

items.title: VIP
items.text: Veterans Independence Program. Tax-free annual funding for home and health support services.

items.title: ETB
items.text: Education and Training Benefit. Taxable education funding with deadlines tied to your release date.

items.title: VEF
items.text: Veterans Emergency Fund. Tax-free emergency help. No other VAC benefit required.

items.title: CF98 / DND 663
items.text: The incident forms completed at the time of a service injury.

items.title: Departmental review
items.text: VAC looking at its own decision again, often with new evidence.

items.title: VRAB
items.text: Veterans Review and Appeal Board. Independent body hearing reviews and appeals of disability decisions.

items.title: BPA
items.text: Bureau of Pensions Advocates. Free lawyers who represent Veterans before VRAB.

items.title: Service Officer
items.text: A trained Legion or War Amps advocate who prepares your application with you at no cost.

items.title: WHERE TO GET HELP
list: Veterans Affairs Canada: 1-866-522-2122
VAC Assistance Service: 1-800-268-7708, 24 hours a day, free and confidential, open to Veterans, former RCMP members, families and caregivers whether or not you are a VAC client.
Legion or War Amps Service Officer: free application assistance, no membership required.
Last Post Fund: 1-800-465-7113, for funeral and burial assistance.

blocks.text: This module contains no VAC rates on purpose. VAC rates change on different schedules, some quarterly. Current figures are published on the VAC rates page at veterans.gc.ca. Check them the day you need them.
If you are in crisis and need to speak with someone now, call or text 988, Canada’s Suicide Crisis Helpline, 24 hours a day in English and French.
